Typeahead suggestions that never wait on the network

The search dialog builds its suggestions locally, from a generated index of page titles and headings, and paints them as soon as you type. An optional server request can supply a different order for the same shortlist, but it is never on the critical path: it goes out after you pause, and it is applied only if it comes back while you are still looking at the same query.

This page demonstrates the timing and the staleness rule. The reordering shown is a fixed illustrative permutation, not the output of any ranker, and nothing here touches the network.

The mechanism, in five rules

  • Local first. Suggestions come from the generated index in the page bundle and render immediately. No request has to finish for the list to appear.
  • Pause, not keystroke. The background request goes out after about 450 ms of idle, so a typed word costs one request rather than one per character.
  • Still current, or discarded. An answer is applied only when its query matches what is on screen. A late answer for a query you have already typed past is dropped rather than reordering the list underneath you.
  • Cached per query. The server keeps the order for a normalized query in a bounded cache (256 entries, 10 minute TTL, least-recently-used eviction), so walking back over a prefix costs nothing.
  • Off by default. The whole path sits behind ORK_SITE_JEV_SUGGEST, which is unset in production. Related pages has its own separate flag, ORK_SITE_JEV_RERANK, and is unaffected either way.

Try the timing

Type, then keep typing without pausing, and watch the status line. The request latency here is simulated at a few hundred milliseconds, which is the order of magnitude a real call takes.

idle
order: local 0 sent · 0 applied · 0 discarded · ~$0.0000

In both modes the local list paints at once, so the difference is entirely in the counters. A request that takes a few hundred milliseconds cannot complete inside a 150 ms per-keystroke abort, so that mode spends money and never applies an order. Moving the call into the background lets the budget be generous, because nothing on screen is waiting for it.

Counting what was sent, not what worked

A request that is aborted client-side has still been sent and is still processed upstream. Charging the estimate only on success makes a path that never completes look free, so the route charges on the attempt and reports attempted, cached and fellBack alongside the items. The counter above follows the same rule: watch the dollar figure climb in the 150 ms mode while nothing is ever applied.
